CP1.02.label: Money is a ledger; the 21 million cap is arithmetic, and the price is discovered by trades.

CP1.04.label: A wallet holds keys, not coins; whoever holds the keys holds the coins.

CP1.06.label: A transaction has no fee field: the fee is the difference between inputs and outputs, implied and never written.

CP1.09.label: Custody: whoever holds the keys holds the coins, exchanges included (Mt. Gox, Tokyo, February 2014).

CP1.11.label: Price is discovered by trades; a day figure is a volume-weighted average.

CP2.02.label: Inputs equal outputs plus the fee: the ledger must balance and the remainder is the miner's fee.

CP2.03.label: How a payment is built: pick coins, write the outputs, leave the fee, sign.

CP2.04.label: How a payment reaches a block: a node relays it, a miner finds a valid nonce and adds a block.

CP2.05.label: Why confirmations: an attacker's chance falls with each block (10 percent attacker: 20.5 to 0.02 percent).

CP2.09.label: Coins are spent whole; a wallet cannot cut a coin in two, so the surplus returns as change.

CP2.10.label: A higher fee rate leaves less change.

CP2.11.label: Only unspent outputs can be spent; wallets and nodes keep exactly that set.

CP2.13.label: Block 74,638 (15 August 2010): a value overflow created about 184 billion bitcoin; a rule was shipped within hours and the honest chain won.

CP2.14.label: In every transaction shape (payment, consolidation, batching) inputs minus outputs is the fee.

CP3.03.label: Release tags sort by number, not by text; release candidates carry rc.

CP3.05.label: An option on the command line overrides the configuration file.

CP3.06.label: Pruning and the transaction index do not mix: the node refuses both at once.

CP3.08.label: rpcauth stores a salted hash, so a leaked configuration file does not reveal the password.

CP3.09.label: Reading a transaction: decode it; the txid ignores the witness, and weight counts it.

CP3.13.label: A reference implementation needs a team and public review, not one keyholder (7 April 2014).

CP3.14.label: Option alertnotify: sends emergency alerts to the owner of the node, usually by email.

CP3.16.label: Option prune: reduces the disk space requirement by deleting old blocks.

CP3.17.label: Option txindex: maintains an index of all transactions, which means a complete copy of the blockchain.

CP3.18.label: Option maxconnections: the maximum number of nodes to accept connections from; it reduces bandwidth use.

CP4.05.label: P2PKH holds only a 20-byte hash of the key, a commitment; the key is revealed only when the coins are spent.

CP4.07.label: A 160-bit hash gives only 80 bits against collisions, which is why SegWit scripts use SHA256.

CP4.09.label: WIF: Base58Check of version 80, the key and a final 01 when compressed.

CP4.10.label: One private key gives two public key encodings and so two addresses; coins sent to one are not seen at the other.

CP4.12.label: Vanity addresses: each further letter divides the chance by 58 and the work cannot be shortcut.

CP4.13.label: A paper wallet must give back its address before any coins are sent.

CP5.03.label: How many words does 256 bits of entropy make? (Code 5)

CP5.05.label: Why does a passphrase change the wallet? (Code 10)

CP5.07.label: How do you know a backup works? (Code 27)

CP5.08.label: A recovery code is entropy in words: 11 bits a word, checksum included.

CP5.09.label: Words become a 512-bit seed by deliberate slowness; a passphrase forks the wallet.

CP5.11.label: A forgotten passphrase loses the funds; the same twelve words with another passphrase give a different wallet.

CP5.15.label: A complete backup: recovery code, passphrase if used, paths or descriptors, other signers' public keys, labels and protocol data; then restore and check the first address.

CP5.17.label: Labels are not derivable from the seed and need their own backup (BIP329).

CP5.18.label: An untested backup file is not an empty one (Mt. Gox, March 2014, about 200,000 bitcoin).

CP5.19.label: Stefan Thomas was paid 7,002 bitcoin in 2011, lost the password and has two guesses left.

CP5.20.label: The gap limit decides how far a recovery scan looks.

CP6.02.label: The sequence field has meant three things, and the lock time is read against the median of eleven blocks.

CP6.04.label: Witnesses in the input script made identifiers malleable; segregated witness moved them out, as a soft fork.

CP6.09.label: A spend updates the UTXO set: remove what is spent, add what is created.

CP6.10.label: The sequence field carries finality, opt-in replacement (BIP125) and a relative timelock (BIP68); bit 31 switches the timelock off.

CP6.13.label: Block 74,638 (15 August 2010): a signed amount needs a range check.

CP6.14.label: Segwit changes the witness but keeps the txid; the wtxid still covers the witness.

CP6.16.label: Mt. Gox blamed malleability (10 February 2014) and researchers checked the claim.

CP6.18.label: The subsidy starts at 50 bitcoin and halves every 210,000 blocks; it reaches zero after block 6,929,999.

CP6.19.label: Weight: each field weighs its bytes times four, except marker, flag and witness (one); 569 weight units, 143 virtual bytes.

CP6.21.label: CompactSize counts: up to 252 one byte, then fd, fe or ff announce two, four or eight more bytes.

CP1.01.label: Origins: block 0 carries a dated headline, and the first payment went from person to person.

CP1.03.label: The network has no bank: every node checks every rule and proof of work makes history costly.

CP1.05.label: A first payment needs an address or invoice, whole coins, change, and a fee for the miner.

CP1.07.label: A double spend is refused by a shared rule, and no bank decides.

CP1.08.label: The key is both the key and the proof of ownership, so it must prove without being shown.

CP1.10.label: Two old solved problems joined in 2008: proof of work (Hashcash, 1997) and agreement without trust (Byzantine Generals, 1982).

CP1.12.label: Bitcoin is virtual, borderless, decentralized and robust, built from a peer-to-peer protocol, a public journal and a consensus rule set.

CP2.01.label: What a payment contains: inputs that spend earlier outputs, outputs for the payee and the change, and a fee.

CP2.06.label: Consensus rules are checked by every node; block 74,638 broke one.

CP2.07.label: The txid is stored in one byte order and printed by explorers in the other; reversing converts between them.

CP2.08.label: Blocks have limited room, so miners pick the best fee rates first.

CP2.12.label: Mining is a search that nobody can shortcut but anyone can check with one hash.

CP3.01.label: Why Bitcoin Core is the reference: it came first, it defines the rules by running them, and it is built in the open.

CP3.02.label: A release you trust: check out a final tag, build it, and compare its hash with the published one.

CP3.04.label: Settings decide what is stored, how much memory is used, and which alerts run.

CP3.07.label: Asking a node: JSON-RPC calls; the cookie or an rpcauth credential lets you in.

CP3.10.label: Weight units: base bytes count four units each, witness bytes one; 194 bytes weigh 569 units, 143 virtual bytes.

CP3.11.label: Checking a block: hash the 80-byte header and rebuild the merkle root yourself.

CP3.12.label: Block timestamps are guesses; Bitcoin Core uses the median time of the last eleven blocks.

CP3.15.label: Option datadir: selects the directory and filesystem for all blockchain data; it needs several gigabytes of free space.

CP3.19.label: Options maxmempool and maxreceivebuffer/maxsendbuffer: limit the transaction memory pool and the per-connection buffers to reduce memory use.

CP4.01.label: A private key is a random number between 1 and n - 1 with 256 bits of entropy.

CP4.02.label: A key must come from a proper random source: only 256 fair coin flips match a Bitcoin key.

CP4.03.label: Public key from private key: multiply G by k with doubling and adding; nobody can run it backwards.

CP4.04.label: Legacy address: HASH160, a version byte and four checksum bytes, written in base58.

CP4.06.label: What P2SH and Bech32 change: P2SH hashes a script; Bech32 and Bech32m add a version, a program and a stronger checksum.

CP4.08.label: Bech32m closes a weakness of Bech32 (an extra q before a final p keeps the checksum valid).

CP4.11.label: A valid address can have no key: a checksum catches typos, not a missing key (the eater address).

CP5.01.label: The deck states that its six Check-yourself questions are the ones the exam will build on.

CP5.02.label: Why is one seed better than many loose keys? (Code 1)

CP5.04.label: What does the checksum protect against? (Code 7)

CP5.10.label: The HD tree gives every purpose a numbered key; hardened steps protect the parent.

CP5.12.label: Where the book differs from the standards: the book's 2,147,483,647 is the largest normal index, not the count of children.

CP5.13.label: Where the book differs from the standards: the book's table uses coin type one for BIP49, the testnet type.

CP5.14.label: Implicit paths need no record (standard); explicit paths must be written down with the code.

CP5.16.label: A typo in a recovery code gives no error but a different, empty wallet.

CP6.01.label: A transaction asks strangers to update their ledgers: inputs point, witnesses prove, outputs assign.

CP6.03.label: An output is an amount and a condition; the fee is a difference, and dust is a policy about everyone's database.

CP6.05.label: The coinbase creates coins under a schedule that ends at block 6,929,999, and weight is what a block is filled by.

CP6.06.label: Two serializations, two identifiers: the legacy hash is the txid, the extended hash is the wtxid.

CP6.07.label: Marker and flag: a legacy parser would read the zero marker as an empty input list.

CP6.08.label: Byte order of the txid in an outpoint is a classic source of mistakes.

CP6.11.label: Lock time: values below 500 million are heights, larger ones are times, read against the median time past.

CP6.12.label: Dust: an output is dust when it costs more to spend than it is worth, at the relay fee; data-carrier outputs are exempt.

CP6.15.label: Segregated witness was a soft fork: old nodes saw anyone-can-spend scripts and accepted the blocks.

CP6.17.label: Coinbase coins are locked for 100 blocks so a reorganisation cannot invalidate coins already spent.

CP6.20.label: A txid is not a field: it is the double SHA-256 of the legacy serialization, shown in reverse byte order.

CP6.22.label: The first spend of an output: ten bitcoins to Hal Finney in block 170 (12 January 2009).

CP6.23.label: The course page asks, as a discussion item, to select one critical issue from the chapter and explain it.

seed_table.mt1:i01:gox-two-events: none: written from the source of the point (the page banks and quizzes hold no question on the Mt. Gox stories)

mt1:i02:toy-chain-supply.stem: Why does the total supply of bitcoin stay just below 21 million?
After how many blocks does the block subsidy halve?
How does the subsidy change over time?

mt1:i03:vwap-third-trade.stem: Why does a pricing service weight each trade's price by its volume?

mt1:i04:fee-not-written.stem: The input is 100,000 satoshis and the outputs are 75,000 and 20,000. What does this program print?
Three outputs are consolidated with a fee of 1,500 satoshis. What does this program print?
A batch pays four employees from one input of 200,000 satoshis with a fee of 3,000. What does this program print?

mt1:i05:change-after-fee-rate.stem: Alice paid 5,000 satoshis for 143 virtual bytes. What does this program print?
A wallet spends one output of 100,000 satoshis, pays 75,000 and leaves a fee of 5,000. What does this program print?
Why does a transaction need a change output at all?

mt1:i06:order-wallet-to-block.stem: Why does a transaction need a change output at all?
Why can two wallets build different transactions for the same payment?

mt1:i07:shop-confirmations.stem: By the whitepaper, an attacker with 10% of the hash power catches up from six blocks behind with probability about:
Why is six confirmations a convention rather than a law?
An attacker holds a tenth of the hash rate and is six blocks behind. What does this program print?

mt1:i08:utxo-set-trace.stem: What does Bitcoin Core do to its UTXO database when a new block arrives?
What does this program print for the shape and fee of Alice's payment?

mt1:i09:conf-precedence-and-refusal.stem: Which value is used when an option is set both in the file and on the command line?
What does this program print when the command line is merged after the file?
Why can the transaction index not be combined with pruning?
A node is configured with prune=5000 and txindex=1. What does Bitcoin Core 31.1 do?

seed_table.mt1:i10:match-node-options: none: written from the source of the point (the option names and purposes come from the owner's 2025 chapter 3 slides; no page question matches situations to options)

mt1:i11:trace-release-tags.stem: Which rule does Mastering Bitcoin give for choosing a release to compile?
What does a release tag attach a version number to?

mt1:i12:rpcauth-and-p2pkh.stem: Which three parts does the value of the option rpcauth have?
Why does the hashed credential protect the file but not the connection?
What does an output that commits to a hash of a key keep hidden until it is spent?
What does a P2PKH address let Alice send instead of Bob's public key?

mt1:i13:vanity-factor.stem: The book's vanity table says an eight-character pattern takes 13 to 18 years on average at 100,000 keys a second. What does its own rule (half the frequency) give?
Is a vanity address less secure than any other address?

mt1:i14:wif-flag-and-balance.stem: A WIF-compressed private key starts with K or L, where a WIF key starts with 5. What causes that?
Why does one private key lead to two different legacy addresses?
What does the wallet import format add to the raw bytes of a private key?
Why is a recovery code alone not always enough to recover a wallet?

mt1:i15:fill-hash-and-collision.stem: What does an output that commits to a hash of a key keep hidden until it is spent?
Why does a 256-bit output not mean 256 bits of security against every attack?

mt1:i16:words-to-entropy.stem: How many words does a BIP39 code have for 128 bits of entropy?
Electrum version 2 uses 132 bits of entropy with an 11-bit word list. How many words is that?
A wallet shows 12 words. How much entropy does that stand for, and how many of the bits are checksum?

seed_table.mt1:i17:match-story-lesson: none: written from the source of the point (the page banks and quizzes hold no question that links these four stories to their lessons)

mt1:i18:trace-gap-limit.stem: A branch received payments at the indices 0, 3 and 25. Which does a scan with a gap limit of 20 find, and where does it stop?

mt1:i19:restore-passphrase-labels.stem: A user mistypes their passphrase during a restoration. What does the wallet show?
What does a seed-only restoration show of a user's history?
Why is a recovery code alone not always enough to recover a wallet?

mt1:i20:trace-compactsize.stem: What is the compactSize encoding of 65536, in hexadecimal?

mt1:i21:trace-sequence-field.stem: Which sequence values signal replaceability under BIP125?
Does a sequence of 0xfffffffe signal replaceability?
How many bits of the sequence carry the relative timelock value?

mt1:i22:overflow-range-check.stem: Why does the amount need a range check if it is a 64-bit integer?

mt1:i23:tracker-legacy-vs-segwit.stem: Why did where a witness is stored turn out to matter?
How do all three malleability problems end for the party that presigned?
Why does a changed signature alter the wtxid but not the txid of a witness transaction?
Which of the two identifiers stays the same when only the witness changes in this program?
